summary: Year 2 children use (not merely define) movement vocabulary: clockwise and anti-clockwise added to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns; a quarter turn linked to a right angle; and multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns that another person can actually follow. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered on still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link bridges to later formal angle work. Guidance keeps turns embodied and routes followable, with feedback on wrong direction or amount.
misconceptions: Clockwise and anti-clockwise confused with each other or with left/right — a new convention on top of frame-dependent left/right
A quarter turn not connected to a right angle — the two treated as separate, unrelated facts
Turn amounts miscounted — a half or a quarter turn produced when a three-quarter turn is asked for
Egocentric direction-giving: routes given from the child's own viewpoint without accounting for the follower's facing

activities.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
steps: Watch a real clock's hands and name the direction they travel as 'clockwise'; then turn your own body a quarter turn clockwise (towards your right, the way the hands would go on a clock lying face-up on the floor and seen from above) and say where you now face.
Make a quarter turn clockwise and mark or point out the corner (angle) between where you started facing and where you finish facing; name it as a right angle.
Make the same quarter turn anti-clockwise and describe how the finishing facing differs.

On a clock face or turn dial, spin an arrow with a 'clockwise, quarter turn' control so it moves 90° and leaves a right-angle mark between start and finish; use 'anti-clockwise' to send it back the other way.
Make two quarter turns clockwise in a row and decide whether that equals one half turn, counting each quarter aloud.
Make a three-quarter turn clockwise, counting the quarters, and point out that three right angles have been passed.
activities.insight: A quarter turn always leaves a right angle between the start and finish arms, and clockwise versus anti-clockwise decides which way you turn — turning fuzzy words into exact instructions.

activities.title: Give and follow a multi-step route that someone else can act on
steps: Guide a partner (or a floor robot) from one point to another using a sequence such as 'forward 2, turn clockwise quarter, forward 3', combining straight-line moves with named turns.
Have the follower act out the route exactly as given, from the follower's own facing, and watch what happens.
On a grid, drive a programmable robot through a maze by stringing moves and turns; a wrong turn direction or wrong amount sends it into a wall, prompting a correction.
Play a barrier game: describe a route to someone who cannot see your map, using direction and turn words precisely enough for them to reproduce it.
When a route 'goes wrong', revise the instructions so the follower, not just you, can reach the target.
activities.insight: Direction and turn words are most useful when they form a sequence another person can follow from their own viewpoint — producing a followable route is the real goal.

activities.title: Check and sort turn and route language
steps: After a stated clockwise or anti-clockwise quarter turn, pick which direction you now face from given options.
Match a quarter turn to one right angle, a half turn to two right angles, and a three-quarter turn to three right angles.
Put a jumbled set of move-and-turn instructions into the order that reaches a target, then test the order by walking or driving it.
activities.insight: You can recognise correct turn facings and the quarter-turn/right-angle link quickly, then confirm sequences by acting them out.

checkQuestion: Give a context and listen for USE: 'Face the window. Make a quarter turn clockwise — which way did you go, and what is the angle you turned through? ... Now guide me from the door to your chair, telling me every move and every turn.' Listen for correct use of clockwise / anti-clockwise, quarter / half / three-quarter, right angle, and a route someone could actually follow.
checkAnswer: Turns the correct direction for clockwise, names the quarter turn as a right angle, and gives the route as a followable sequence using correct directional and turn vocabulary — adjusted so that the follower, not just the child, can act on it.
